objective: By the end of this lesson you can explain, demonstrate from the right seat and teach straight climbs, climbing turns and level-offs in a single-engine airplane, and spot, explain and fix the climb errors learners make most.
why: Every flight starts with a climb, and a climb is where power is high, airspeed is low and the nose hides the sky ahead, so left-turning tendencies, stall risk and traffic all peak together [[24:80|AFH 3-19]] [[24:123|AFH 5-18]] [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]]. The habits a learner builds here, pitch for airspeed, right rudder and an outside scan, carry into every departure [[24:78|AFH 3-17]].

warmup: Think first: your learner climbs with the airspeed swinging 10 knots either side of the target while the heading creeps left. Is that one error or two? Where would you look first, the nose, the wingtips or the instruments, to find out, and what would you say before touching the controls?

key_terms.def: A climb at the manufacturer's recommended speed, generally faster than VY, for better engine cooling, control authority and view over the nose [[24:78|AFH 3-17]].
Best rate of climb speed: the most altitude gained in a given time [[24:78|AFH 3-17]].
Best angle of climb speed: the most altitude gained over a given horizontal distance [[24:78|AFH 3-17]].
The altitude where VX and VY meet and the airplane cannot climb higher, because no excess power is left [[24:78|AFH 3-17]] [[1:264|PHAK 11-8]].
The altitude where the airplane can no longer climb faster than 100 fpm [[1:264|PHAK 11-8]].
Thrust or power beyond what level flight needs. Climb angle depends on excess thrust, climb rate on excess power [[1:121|PHAK 5-24]] [[1:264|PHAK 11-8]].
Asymmetric propeller loading: at high angle of attack the descending right blade makes more thrust, yawing the nose left [[24:80|AFH 3-19]] [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]].
To the pilot, four elements: torque reaction, corkscrew slipstream, gyroscopic action and P-factor [[1:127|PHAK 5-30]] [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]].
In steeper turns the outside wing moves faster and makes more lift, so the bank tends to increase unless opposite aileron is used [[24:75|AFH 3-14]].
Teaching each maneuver by outside references and flight instruments together, with the same control use either way [[24:66|AFH 3-5]] [[25:180|AIH 9-10]].
A feeling of tumbling backward after an abrupt change from climb to level flight, which can lead a pilot to push the nose too low [[1:430|PHAK 17-8]].
Accurate perception and understanding of all the factors that affect safety before, during and after the flight [[25:17|AIH 1-13]].

chunks.title: Why we teach climbs, and where they fit

body.p: Every flight climbs. After takeoff the pilot usually climbs at VY until it is safe to change to a normal or cruise climb [[24:78|AFH 3-17]]. The other fundamentals are variations of straight-and-level flight [[24:67|AFH 3-6]], so this lesson builds directly on straight-and-level flight (AI.VIII.A) and level turns (AI.VIII.B).

The purpose, in the AFH's words, is that the pilot knows the engine power settings, natural-horizon pitch attitudes and flight instrument indications that give each type of climb [[24:78|AFH 3-17]]. Your learner should finish able to set any climb by picture and power, not by chasing a needle.

bullets: Entry: gently raise the nose to the climb attitude against the natural horizon while adding climb power at the same time [[24:80|AFH 3-19]].
Hold: wingtips for bank, nose for pitch, instruments to confirm; power stays fixed at climb power and airspeed is controlled with elevator; trim nose-up [[24:80|AFH 3-19]].
Level-off: start about 10 percent of the climb rate before the target altitude, lower the nose slowly, keep climb power until cruise speed, then set cruise power and retrim [[24:81|AFH 3-20]].
Climbing turn: climb first and then bank, or do both together; keep the bank shallow and constant, the airspeed constant and the controls coordinated [[24:81|AFH 3-20]].

callout.text: The CFI ACS lists no numeric tolerances for this Task. You must explain while you demonstrate, and the examiner must pick at least one Task from Area VIII (ACS AI.VIII.C and the Area VIII Note).

check.q: A learner asks why you practice climbs at altitude when every takeoff already has one. Your short answer?
check.a: To learn the power setting, horizon picture and instrument indications for each kind of climb [[24:78|AFH 3-17]], built on the straight-and-level skills already learned [[24:67|AFH 3-6]]. Then every departure uses them (application).

chunks.title: What changes when the nose comes up

body.p: Back pressure raises the angle of attack, so for a moment lift is greater than weight and the airplane starts up. Once the flight path is steady on its upward slope, angle of attack and lift go back to about their level-flight values [[1:120|PHAK 5-23]] [[1:121|PHAK 5-24]].

What stays changed is drag. On an upward path part of the weight acts rearward, along with drag. With no added power the airspeed bleeds off until drag again equals thrust at a lower speed [[1:121|PHAK 5-24]]. That is why the AFH has climb power go in together with the pitch change [[24:80|AFH 3-19]].

A climb is held up by excess thrust. A 10° climb needs thrust equal to drag plus 17 percent of weight, and when the excess thrust is gone the airplane has reached its absolute ceiling [[1:121|PHAK 5-24]]. Rate of climb depends on excess power: in the PHAK example a 200 hp engine using 130 hp for level flight has 70 hp left to climb with [[1:262|PHAK 11-6]].

A zoom climb is different: power stays the same and airspeed is traded for altitude, so the airspeed keeps falling [[1:262|PHAK 11-6]] [[1:263|PHAK 11-7]]. Make sure learners know a sustained climb needs power, not just pitch.

callout.text: A simple way to say it: the wing makes about the same lift as in level flight; the extra power is what does the climbing [[1:121|PHAK 5-24]]. The AFH words it as needing excess lift and more power for the extra induced drag [[24:78|AFH 3-17]]. Both books agree a sustained climb needs excess thrust.

check.q: Your learner raises the nose to the climb picture but leaves cruise power set. What happens to airspeed, and why?
check.a: It decays, because part of the weight now acts with drag, until drag and thrust balance at a lower speed [[1:121|PHAK 5-24]].

chunks.title: Cruise climb, VY or VX: choosing the speed

head: Climb
What it gives
When
rows: Normal (cruise) climb
The manufacturer's speed, usually above VY: better engine cooling, more control authority, better view over the nose [[24:78|AFH 3-17]]
En route climbs once clear of obstacles; a normal climb is sometimes called cruise climb [[24:78|AFH 3-17]]
Best rate (VY)
Most altitude in a given time [[24:78|AFH 3-17]]
Leaving a runway without obstructions until it is safe to change to a cruise climb [[24:78|AFH 3-17]]; getting to an assigned altitude quickly [[1:263|PHAK 11-7]]
Best angle (VX)
Most altitude over a given horizontal distance; steeper, but slower to reach altitude [[24:78|AFH 3-17]]
Clearing obstacles such as a strand of trees after takeoff [[24:78|AFH 3-17]]

body.p: As altitude increases, VX increases and VY decreases until they meet at the absolute ceiling [[24:78|AFH 3-17]]. The service ceiling is the altitude where the airplane can no longer climb faster than 100 fpm [[1:264|PHAK 11-8]]. More weight, more altitude, gear down or flaps down all cut excess power, so both climbs get worse, and a heavier airplane needs a higher speed for its smaller best rate [[1:264|PHAK 11-8]]. Have learners use the AFM/POH charts for the speed that fits the day [[24:78|AFH 3-17]].

VX and VY on takeoff, ground effect and the ±5 knot standard are covered in AI.VII.A (Normal Takeoff and Climb). The point here is the en route choice. The AFH notes that a VY climb needs a much quicker response to a power failure, and suggests a lower-pitch cruise climb [[24:137|AFH 6-5]].
Accuracy pays: the AIH says correct power settings and climb speeds, plus accurate heading control in the climb, give a measurable increase in climb performance [[25:180|AIH 9-10]].

check.q: On a hot day your learner holds VY all the way from pattern altitude to 7,500 feet. What do you suggest instead, and what two benefits do you name?
check.a: A normal (cruise) climb at the manufacturer's speed: better engine cooling and a better view over the nose, plus more control authority [[24:78|AFH 3-17]].

chunks.title: Entering and holding a straight climb: attitude, power, trim

bullets: Clear first. The learner should use a clearing procedure before every training maneuver [[24:33|AFH 1-12]].
Propeller first: with a controllable-pitch propeller, advance the propeller control before adding power [[24:80|AFH 3-19]].

Attitude and power together: gentle back pressure to the climb attitude on the natural horizon while adding climb power [[24:80|AFH 3-19]]. Set cowl flaps, if installed, to keep cylinder head temperatures within limits [[24:80|AFH 3-19]].
Expect the nose to rise: more slipstream over the horizontal stabilizer can pitch it up more than wanted, so be ready with the needed pressure [[24:80|AFH 3-19]].
Right rudder, and some aileron, for torque and P-factor [[24:80|AFH 3-19]].
Hold and trim: as speed decays the nose tends to drop unless back pressure increases, so trim nose-up until the attitude holds without pressure [[24:80|AFH 3-19]].
Pitch for airspeed: power stays at climb power and airspeed is controlled with elevator; check the horizon for pitch, the wingtips for bank, then the instruments [[24:80|AFH 3-19]].

Hold the power: a normally aspirated engine loses power as it climbs (RPM falls with a fixed-pitch propeller, manifold pressure with a controllable one), so keep advancing the throttle [[24:80|AFH 3-19]].

body.p: Trim the AFH way: set the attitude, hold it with control pressure, then trim the pressure out. Flying the airplane with the trim is a common fault even for experienced pilots [[24:71|AFH 3-10]]. If rudder and aileron trim exist, trim rudder, then elevator, then aileron, but only after airspeed and pitch are constant [[24:71|AFH 3-10]].

On the instruments the same climb shows the VSI trending up and then settling at a rate that fits the airspeed and attitude. Once stable, the airspeed indicator is primary for pitch and the tachometer or manifold pressure gauge for power [[23:175|IFH 7-14]].

callout.text: Nose up and power up together, right rudder, trim it off. Then pitch for airspeed while the power stays put [[24:80|AFH 3-19]].

check.q: Climb power is set and the airspeed has settled 8 knots below the target. Which control does the learner use?
check.a: The elevator: lower the nose slightly. With power fixed, airspeed is controlled by pitch [[24:80|AFH 3-19]].

body.p: The PHAK splits what pilots call "torque" into four elements [[1:127|PHAK 5-30]] [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]]. All four are strong in a climb, where power is high and airspeed is low.

head: Element
What it does in the climb
Correction
rows: Torque reaction
The engine and propeller turn one way, so the airplane tends to roll the other way: left, with a clockwise propeller [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]] [[24:80|AFH 3-19]]
Aileron pressure; the built-in compensation is set for cruise speed only [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]]
Corkscrew (spiraling) slipstream
Compact at high power and low speed; it strikes the vertical fin and yaws the nose [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]]
Rudder, as needed at the time [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]]
Gyroscopic precession
A pitch or yaw change acts 90° ahead in the direction of rotation, causing yaw or pitch [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]] [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]]
Elevator and rudder; smooth pitch changes [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]]
P-factor
At high angle of attack the descending right blade takes a bigger bite, moving thrust to the right and yawing the nose left [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]] [[24:80|AFH 3-19]]
Right rudder pressure [[24:80|AFH 3-19]]

body.p: Net effect in a climb: torque and P-factor roll and yaw the airplane to the left, so the pilot holds right rudder and aileron pressure [[24:80|AFH 3-19]]. The amounts change with power, speed and attitude, so the pilot keeps adjusting [[1:129|PHAK 5-32]].

Tell the learner it will feel awkward at first and become instinctive with practice [[24:80|AFH 3-19]]. The usual sign it is missing is yaw in the climb from too little right rudder, which is on the AFH error list [[24:81|AFH 3-20]].

callout.text: Do not chase rudder trim during the climb entry. Trimming rudder while airspeed is changing only adds workload, and in many propeller airplanes the built-in compensation makes it impractical [[24:71|AFH 3-10]].

check.q: Why does a trainer that flies hands-off in cruise need right rudder in the climb?
check.a: Its built-in compensation cancels torque at cruise speed only [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]]. At climb power, low speed and high angle of attack, P-factor and torque yaw and roll it left [[24:80|AFH 3-19]].

chunks.title: Climbing turns: bank, back pressure and coordination

bullets: Same power and pitch cannot hold the straight-climb airspeed in a bank; the airplane climbs at a slightly shallower angle because some lift is turning it [[24:81|AFH 3-20]].
Steep banks cut the climb rate sharply. Keep a shallow, constant bank; a medium or steep bank can leave little or no climb [[24:81|AFH 3-20]].
Hold a constant airspeed and rate of turn, left and right. Coordination is a primary factor [[24:81|AFH 3-20]].
Entry: climb first then bank, or climb and turn together. Add pitch for the lost vertical lift, and a little more back pressure again for the extra drag of the climb [[24:81|AFH 3-20]].

body.p: Everything from level turns still applies: inherent stability, overbanking, adverse yaw, propeller effects, less vertical lift and more drag [[24:81|AFH 3-20]]. Below about 20° of bank the airplane tends to roll level unless aileron is held; from 20° to 45° it holds its bank; from about 45° it tends to overbank and needs opposite aileron [[24:73|AFH 3-12]]. Overbanking comes from the outside wing moving faster and making more lift [[24:75|AFH 3-14]].

Left and right feel different. Rolling right at low speed and high power, adverse yaw adds to the left yaw of P-factor, so it takes a lot of right rudder. Rolling left, P-factor cancels some adverse yaw, so less right rudder is needed [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

bullets: Nose moves before the bank starts: rudder too soon [[24:77|AFH 3-16]].
Bank starts before the nose moves, or the nose swings the wrong way: rudder too late [[24:77|AFH 3-16]].
Nose rises or drops as the bank starts: too much or too little back pressure [[24:77|AFH 3-16]].
Pressed to the outside of the turn is a skid; pressed to the inside is a slip [[24:74|AFH 3-13]].
From the left seat the nose seems to rise in left turns and drop in right turns (parallax), so each direction has its own sight picture [[24:76|AFH 3-15]].

callout.text: A slip in a climbing turn can cancel the climb, leaving little or no altitude gain [[24:81|AFH 3-20]]. Holding uncoordinated control deflections in a turn can set up a spin, worst at low altitude such as in the pattern [[24:73|AFH 3-12]].

check.q: Your learner rolls into a right climbing turn at VY and the ball slides toward the low (right) wing. What is it, and what do you say?
check.a: A slip, ball to the inside of the turn [[24:74|AFH 3-13]]. Add right rudder: rolling right at low speed and high power needs substantial right rudder [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

body.p: Start before the target altitude, at about 10 percent of the rate of climb: at 500 fpm, begin 50 feet early [[24:81|AFH 3-20]]. The IFH uses the same lead and explains it: the airplane keeps climbing at a decreasing rate through the transition [[23:177|IFH 7-16]].

bullets: Lower the nose smoothly and slowly so airspeed can build; pitching down quickly without the speed can lose altitude [[24:81|AFH 3-20]].
Keep climb power for now so the airplane accelerates [[24:81|AFH 3-20]].
Expect steady pitch and rudder changes as the speed increases [[23:177|IFH 7-16]].
At cruise airspeed, set cruise power and the propeller, if equipped, then retrim [[24:81|AFH 3-20]].

body.p: To level at climb airspeed instead, lower the nose to the level attitude for that speed and reduce power at the same time. If power comes off in step with the pitch change, the airspeed stays constant [[23:177|IFH 7-16]].

callout.text: Too much forward pressure at level-off loses altitude or gives an uncomfortable low-G feel [[24:81|AFH 3-20]]. An abrupt change from climb to level can also cause the inversion illusion, a feeling of tumbling backward that tempts the pilot to push the nose lower still [[1:430|PHAK 17-8]].

check.q: Your learner is climbing at 800 fpm to 4,500 feet. When does the level-off start, and what is the throttle doing for the next minute?
check.a: About 80 feet early, near 4,420 feet (10 percent of 800). Climb power stays in until cruise airspeed, then cruise power and retrim [[24:81|AFH 3-20]].

chunks.title: Visual references and integrated flight instruction

body.p: Attitude is the angle between the airplane's axes and the natural horizon. Flying visually, the pilot judges it from the wings and cowling against the horizon [[24:65|AFH 3-4]].

head: Reference
What the learner uses in a climb
rows: Pitch
A chosen point on the nose held at the climb position against the natural horizon, then cross-checked on the instruments [[24:80|AFH 3-19]] [[24:69|AFH 3-8]]
Bank (straight)
Both wingtips, equal against the horizon; the nose alone lets small bank errors go unnoticed [[24:80|AFH 3-19]] [[24:69|AFH 3-8]]
Bank (turns)
The flat top of the cowling against the horizon sets the bank; then a glance at the attitude indicator [[24:76|AFH 3-15]]
Heading
Two points lined up ahead; over water or flat snow, the magnetic heading indication [[24:69|AFH 3-8]]
Sound and feel
In a fixed-pitch airplane engine sound falls as the pitch rises; air noise falls as the nose rises and speed drops [[24:64|AFH 3-3]]

body.p: Integrated flight instruction means using outside references and flight instruments together. About 90 percent of attention goes outside to the horizon and traffic, and no more than about 10 percent inside [[24:66|AFH 3-5]] [[24:67|AFH 3-6]]. A pitch change of several inches on the horizon may show as a tiny move on the attitude indicator [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].

The AIH adds that instrument references should start the first time each maneuver is introduced, with the same control use whichever reference is used [[25:180|AIH 9-10]] [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]. Make sure learners understand it does not prepare them for flight in IMC [[25:181|AIH 9-11]] [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].

bullets: Reference lines: a dry-erase marker or removable tape on the windshield or cowling; horizontal lines are best set in flight [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].
Instrument covers for the first hours, or to break an instrument-fixation habit [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].
Same seat position every flight, since the references depend on it [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].

check.q: What does the AFH call the most common beginner error with references, and what tool does it suggest?
check.a: Making pitch or bank corrections while still looking inside. Instrument covers force the learner onto outside references [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].

body.p: Situational awareness is an accurate picture of all the factors affecting the flight. A situationally aware pilot is not fixated on one item; distractions that start as a minor problem, like an odd gauge, have caused accidents when the pilot stopped controlling the aircraft [[25:17|AIH 1-13]].

head: Hazard
In this Task
How you teach it
rows: Distractions
A gauge, chart or radio call pulls the eyes inside while the nose is high and the speed is low [[25:17|AIH 1-13]]
Practice dividing attention with planned distractions; the AIH list includes reading the OAT and a 200-foot climb and level-off [[25:180|AIH 9-10]]
Task prioritization
Application: workload builds in a departure climb (radios, checklist, traffic, engine gauges)
Plan, prioritize and sequence tasks; when overloaded, stop, think, slow down and prioritize [[1:63|PHAK 2-24]]. Once airborne, budget time and prioritize [[30:47|RMH 6-4]]
Loss of situational awareness
Fixating on the airspeed or the nose and losing traffic, altitude or position [[25:17|AIH 1-13]]
Ask about traffic, engine indications and position during the climb [[25:18|AIH 1-14]]
Disorientation
Inversion illusion at an abrupt level-off; a false horizon from a sloping cloud layer [[1:430|PHAK 17-8]]
Smooth level-offs, and cross-check instruments when the horizon is poor [[24:67|AFH 3-6]]

body.p: Climbing turns add body sensations: postural signals become false when forces overpower gravity, and climbing turns are one of the listed cases [[1:430|PHAK 17-8]]. The leans can follow a slow, unnoticed turn once the wings are leveled [[1:429|PHAK 17-7]].

Why it matters here: secondary tasks raise the risk of an inadvertent stall [[25:180|AIH 9-10]], and power-on stalls are practiced from straight climbs and climbing turns of 15° to 20° bank because accidental stalls happen in climbs and when clearing obstacles [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

callout.text: Time the distractions. In the cognitive stage, distractions make performance fall apart; in the associative stage the learner copes better [[25:75|AIH 3-24]]. Add them once the climb is consistent.

check.q: When do you start adding distractions to climbing turns, and why then?
check.a: Once performance is consistent (associative stage). Earlier, distractions just make the skill fall apart [[25:75|AIH 3-24]]; later they train divided attention and stall awareness [[25:180|AIH 9-10]].

chunks.title: Collision hazards in a nose-high climb

body.p: The climb attitude hides the sky ahead: the AIM lists aircraft attitude as a source of extra blind spots, along with high or low wings and windshield posts [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]]. A cruise climb gives a better view over the nose [[24:78|AFH 3-17]].

bullets: During climbs, when traffic can be seen, make gentle banks left and right often enough to keep scanning the airspace [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15]].

Clear before every turn: in a high-wing airplane raise the wing toward the turn and look; in a low-wing airplane lower it and look. Clearing comes before climbs and all other maneuvers [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]].
Have learners call "clear" left, right, above or below out loud [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15]].

Lower the pitch a little now and then: AC 90-48E suggests adjusting the pitch attitude in a climb to see over the nose. It also notes that a low-wing airplane above a high-wing one is the worst case for blind spots [[16:13|AC 90-48E 12.1]].
Scan in short movements of no more than 10°, holding each area at least 1 second. Traffic with no relative motion that grows larger is on a collision course: act at once [[24:32|AFH 1-11]].
ADS-B In helps, but not every aircraft shows on it, and staring at a display is its own hazard [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]].

body.p: Most midair collisions happen in good VFR weather, in daylight, within 5 miles of an airport [[24:31|AFH 1-10]]. In the AIH study, a flight instructor was on board in 37 percent, and most happened at or near nontowered airports below 1,000 feet [[25:181|AIH 9-11]]. That is departure climb territory.

callout.text: When weather permits, every pilot must keep watch to see and avoid other aircraft, IFR or VFR [[60:447|14 CFR 91.113(b)]].

body.p: Make the learner own the scan. A learner who thinks the instructor handles traffic never builds the habit, and any maneuver started without clearing should be corrected at once [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

check.q: Your learner holds a perfect wings-level VY climb for three minutes on departure. What clearing technique is missing?
check.a: Gentle banks left and right during the climb so the airspace ahead of the nose can be scanned [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15]].

body.p: On the ground, brief the objectives and completion standards, the steps, the end result and the safety items [[25:175|AIH 9-5]]. For this lesson that means the climb power and nose picture for cruise climb, VY and VX in your trainer, the 10 percent level-off lead, and the clearing plan. The ACS gives no tolerance here, so set and state your own standard.

Sequence it: known to unknown, building climbs on straight-and-level flight and level turns, and simple to complex, with straight climbs before climbing turns [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]. Each block should be mastered and then combined with the next [[25:146|AIH 7-2]].

head: Step
In the climbs lesson
rows: Instructor tells, instructor does

Demonstrate a straight climb from cruise while naming the power setting, the nose picture, the right rudder and the trim, then the level-off lead. Fly it exactly as explained; if it strays, say so right away [[25:177|AIH 9-7]] [[24:80|AFH 3-19]]
Learner tells, instructor does
The learner calls each step and the level-off altitude while you fly. A belief like "low airspeed means add power" shows up before the learner is busy flying [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]
Learner tells, learner does
The learner flies and talks. You can tell whether a wing-low climb comes from a misconception or from motor skill [[25:178|AIH 9-8]]
Learner does, instructor evaluates
Straight climbs, climbing turns both ways and level-offs to assigned altitudes, judged against the standards you briefed [[25:175|AIH 9-5]]

bullets: Feel: point out the sound and seat-pressure changes, and teach the learner to perceive and react to them, not just notice them [[24:64|AFH 3-3]].
Feedback right away: do not let learners practice mistakes; unlearning is harder than learning it right [[25:76|AIH 3-25]].
Both directions: practicing turns one way only is a listed level-turn error [[24:78|AFH 3-17]], and right and left climbing turns need different rudder [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].
Correlate: once climbs are consistent, tie them to departures and cruise-climb choices, the correlation level of learning [[25:66|AIH 3-15]].

check.q: While you fly, the learner talks you through it and says "airspeed is low, add power." What misconception did you just catch, and what is the rule?
check.a: In the climb, power stays at climb power and pitch controls airspeed [[24:80|AFH 3-19]]. Catching it while you fly is the point of that step [[25:178|AIH 9-8]].

body.p: The first ten rows are the AFH list for climbs and climbing turns [[24:81|AFH 3-20]]; the last three come from the AFH attitude-flying and trim pages. The "what you see" and "fix" columns use the AFH text around them.

head: Error
What you see
How to fix it
rows: Setting pitch from the airspeed indicator and chasing it
Head down, nose bobbing, airspeed swinging around the target
Set the attitude on the horizon, hold it, then check the airspeed; small pitch changes [[24:80|AFH 3-19]] [[24:67|AFH 3-6]]
Too aggressive elevator, excessive climb angle
Nose far above the climb picture, airspeed decaying
Gentle back pressure to the known climb attitude; demonstrate the picture again [[24:80|AFH 3-19]]
Inadequate or wrong rudder in climbing turns
Ball off center in the turn
Rudder with aileron; more right rudder rolling right, less rolling left [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]
Yaw in the straight climb
Nose and heading creep left
Right rudder pressure for P-factor and torque [[24:80|AFH 3-19]]
Fixation on the nose
Climbing with one wing low
Wingtips are the primary bank reference [[24:69|AFH 3-8]]
Uncoordinated entry to the climbing turn
No turn, just a climb with one wing low
Coordinated aileron and rudder; read the nose on entry [[24:77|AFH 3-16]]
Slip counteracting the climb
Little or no altitude gain in the turn
Center the ball with rudder [[24:74|AFH 3-13]]
Pitch and bank not held constant in the turn
Bank and nose wander
Shallow, constant bank on the cowling reference; trim [[24:76|AFH 3-15]] [[24:71|AFH 3-10]]
Asking more than the airplane can climb
Airspeed decaying, little climb, often with a steep bank or high, heavy conditions
Proper speed and shallow bank; use the POH charts [[24:78|AFH 3-17]] [[1:264|PHAK 11-8]]
Too much forward pressure at level-off
Altitude loss or a low-G feel
Smooth, slow pitch change starting at the 10 percent lead [[24:81|AFH 3-20]]
Flying with the trim
Constant trim wheel movement while speed changes
Attitude first, hold, then trim the pressure off [[24:71|AFH 3-10]]
Correcting while looking inside
Eyes on the panel during each correction
About 90 percent outside; instrument covers if needed [[24:66|AFH 3-5]] [[24:67|AFH 3-6]]
Leaning away from the turn
Head and body tilted toward the high wing
Correct it at once so the references read right [[24:76|AFH 3-15]]

body.p: On the checkride the examiner may play a learner with a simulated error. Name what you see, give the likely cause, demonstrate the fix, then let the "learner" try again. That matches the AIH reteaching cycle: demonstrate, practice under direction, evaluate [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

check.q: Your learner's straight climb drifts 10° left each minute with the left wing slightly low. Which listed errors and what fix?
check.a: Too little right rudder (yaw) and fixation on the nose (wing low) [[24:81|AFH 3-20]]. Fix with right rudder pressure and the wingtips as the bank reference [[24:80|AFH 3-19]] [[24:69|AFH 3-8]].

f1.caption: Figure 5-36. Changes in lift during climb entry. Figure 5-37. Changes in speed during climb entry.
f1.alt: Left: an airplane goes from level flight (normal lift) to climb entry (increased lift, longer lift arrow) to a steady climb (normal lift again). Right: level flight with forces balanced at constant speed; climb entry where drag is greater than thrust and speed is slowing; steady climb with forces balanced at constant speed. Thrust, drag, lift and weight arrows are drawn on each airplane.

f2.caption: Figure 3-19. Best angle of climb verses best rate of climb.
f2.alt: Two climb paths from the same runway. The steeper yellow path is labeled best angle-of-climb airspeed (VX), the greatest altitude gain in the shortest horizontal distance. The shallower red path is labeled best rate-of-climb airspeed (VY), the greatest altitude gain in the shortest time. Trees stand beyond the runway.

f3.caption: Figure 3-21. Climb indications.
f3.alt: Two views over the nose of a high-wing trainer in a climb, with the nose above the horizon. Left: a six-pack of round gauges (airspeed, attitude indicator showing nose up, altimeter, turn coordinator, heading indicator, vertical speed). Right: the same climb on a glass primary flight display.

f4.caption: Figure 5-51. Asymmetrical loading of propeller (P-factor).
f4.alt: Two side views of a propeller and nose. At low angle of attack the load arrows on the upward and downward moving blades are equal. At high angle of attack the arrow on the downward moving blade is longer than the one on the upward moving blade.

f5.caption: Figure 3-13. Indications of a slip and skid.
f5.alt: Three panels. Skid: ball to the outside of the turn, pilot feels a sideways force to the outside. Coordinated turn: ball centered, force straight down into the seat. Slip: ball to the inside of the turn, pilot feels a sideways force to the inside. Each panel shows an attitude indicator and a turn coordinator.

f6.caption: Figure 3-5. Integrated flight instruction teaches pilots to use both external and instrument attitude references.
f6.alt: A pie chart over a view out a high-wing cabin window and an instrument panel: 90 percent of the pilot's attention outside the flight deck, no more than 10 percent inside.

f7.caption: Figure 1-11. Proper scanning techniques can mitigate midair collisions. Pilots should be aware of potential blind spots and attempt to clear the entire area in which they are maneuvering.
f7.alt: A low-wing airplane above a high-wing airplane, with a shaded area between them labeled blind spots: each pilot's wing hides the other airplane.

scenario.title: Climbing turns over a busy, hazy practice area
scenario.setup: Your learner has 6 hours in a fixed-pitch, high-wing trainer and fixated on the attitude indicator last lesson. It is a hot afternoon near maximum weight. The practice area is 8 miles from a nontowered airport, several training airplanes are on the CTAF, haze softens the horizon, and a cloud layer slopes away to the west. Today's plan: straight climbs and climbing turns from 3,000 to 5,500 feet.

questions.q: What do you brief about attitude references, given the haze and the sloping clouds?
questions.a: Natural horizon first, about 90 percent outside, instruments to confirm [[24:66|AFH 3-5]] [[24:67|AFH 3-6]]. Warn that a sloping cloud layer can give a false horizon [[1:430|PHAK 17-8]], and that if no horizon can be seen it is IMC for practical purposes, which integrated instruction does not prepare them for [[24:65|AFH 3-4]] [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].

questions.q: Which climb speed do you choose for the long climbs, and why today?
questions.a: A normal (cruise) climb: better engine cooling and view over the nose [[24:78|AFH 3-17]]. Heat and weight also cut excess power, so climb performance is lower today [[1:264|PHAK 11-8]].

questions.q: The learner climbs straight ahead at VY with eyes on the airspeed indicator. What collision risk do you point out, and what do you teach?
questions.a: The nose-high attitude adds blind spots [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]]. Teach gentle banks left and right during the climb [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15]], a 10°, 1-second scan [[24:32|AFH 1-11]], and remind them most midairs happen near airports in good weather [[24:31|AFH 1-10]].

questions.q: In a left climbing turn the learner banks 35° and the VSI shows almost no climb. What do you explain?
questions.a: Steep banks sharply cut the climb rate; medium or steep banks can leave little or no climb, so keep it shallow [[24:81|AFH 3-20]]. Today's heat and weight already cut excess power [[1:264|PHAK 11-8]].

questions.q: You ask the learner to find the CTAF on the chart during a climbing turn. The nose creeps up and the stall warning sounds. What is happening, and what next?
questions.a: A secondary task raises the risk of an inadvertent stall [[25:180|AIH 9-10]]; climbs and climbing turns are where accidental power-on stalls happen [[24:123|AFH 5-18]]. Be ready to take the controls, then teach the learner to divide attention, flying the attitude first.

questions.q: At level-off the learner shoves the nose down hard and says it felt like going over backward. What do you explain, and what technique fixes it?
questions.a: The inversion illusion from an abrupt climb-to-level change [[1:430|PHAK 17-8]]. Start at the 10 percent lead and lower the nose smoothly and slowly [[24:81|AFH 3-20]].

skills.do: From the right seat, demonstrate and explain a straight climb and a climbing turn at the speed the examiner names (cruise climb, VY or VX from the POH), then level off at an assigned altitude, with clearing first. The ACS lists no numeric tolerance for this Task, so show smooth, coordinated control and say the power, attitude, rudder, trim and level-off lead as you fly (ACS AI.VIII.C.S1).
skills.practice: Fly climbs with a pilot friend in the left seat and talk the whole time: power with the pitch change, right rudder, trim, 10 percent lead, climb power until cruise speed [[24:80|AFH 3-19]] [[24:81|AFH 3-20]]. Practice turns both ways at a shallow bank [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

skills.do: The examiner, playing your learner, flies climbs with errors such as chasing the airspeed, a wing-low climb, a slipping climbing turn or a hard level-off. Name what you see, explain the cause, demonstrate the fix and coach a retry (ACS AI.VIII.C.S2).
skills.practice: For each row of the error table, practice saying "what I see, why, the fix" in one breath, then fly the fix [[24:81|AFH 3-20]] [[25:181|AIH 9-11]].

quiz.q: In a steady climb at constant airspeed, how does wing lift compare with level flight at the same airspeed, per the PHAK?
options: About 17 percent more than in level flight
More than level flight by the amount of excess thrust
About the same as in level flight once the climb is steady
More, because the angle of attack stays raised
quiz.why: Lift and angle of attack go back to about level-flight values once the climb is stable; the momentary increase is only at entry [[1:120|PHAK 5-23]] [[1:121|PHAK 5-24]].

quiz.q: Climb power is set and fixed, and the airspeed is 5 knots fast. What does the learner adjust?
options: Reduce power slightly with the throttle
Raise the nose slightly with elevator
Add nose-down trim and wait for it
Reduce power and lower the nose together
quiz.why: Throughout the climb, with power fixed at climb power, airspeed is controlled with elevator [[24:80|AFH 3-19]].

quiz.q: As altitude increases, what happens to VX and VY?
options: Both decrease at the same rate until they meet
VX decreases while VY increases until they meet
Both stay the same as indicated airspeeds
VX increases and VY decreases until they meet
quiz.why: VX increases and VY decreases with altitude, and they meet at the absolute ceiling [[24:78|AFH 3-17]].

quiz.q: Climbing at 600 fpm, when should the learner begin to level off for 6,000 feet?
options: At about 5,940 feet
At about 5,880 feet, 20 percent early
At about 5,994 feet, 1 percent early
At 6,000 feet, then lower the nose
quiz.why: Lead by about 10 percent of the rate of climb: 600 x 0.10 = 60 feet, so 6,000 - 60 = 5,940 feet [[24:81|AFH 3-20]].

quiz.q: Why does the nose often pitch up more than wanted as climb power goes in?
options: Gyroscopic precession acting on the propeller disc
The center of gravity moving aft with power
More slipstream over the horizontal stabilizer
P-factor moving the thrust line upward
quiz.why: In many airplanes the added slipstream over the horizontal stabilizer raises the pitch attitude more than desired [[24:80|AFH 3-19]].

quiz.q: In which climbing-turn entry does the AFH say substantial right rudder is needed?
options: Rolling left at low airspeed and high power
Rolling right at low airspeed and high power
Rolling either way at cruise airspeed and power
Rolling left with the power at idle
quiz.why: Rolling right, adverse yaw adds to P-factor's left yaw; rolling left, P-factor cancels some adverse yaw [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].

quiz.q: Which statement about bank in a climbing turn matches the AFH?
options: Use a medium bank so the airplane holds the bank by itself
Use about 45° so the turn finishes before the climb does
Bank has no effect on climb rate if power stays constant
Keep it shallow; steeper banks may leave little or no climb
quiz.why: Steep banks significantly decrease the rate of climb; shallow banks give an efficient climb, and medium or steep banks may give none [[24:81|AFH 3-20]].

quiz.q: What does the AIM say pilots should do during climbs in conditions that permit seeing traffic?
options: Make gentle banks left and right to keep scanning the sky
Climb only at VX to shorten the time in the climb
Hold the wings level so others can predict the path
Look mainly ahead, since traffic from the sides is rare
quiz.why: During climbs and descents, execute gentle banks left and right at a frequency that permits continuous scanning [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15]].

quiz.q: A learner's straight climb drifts left with the left wing a little low. Which AFH-listed errors fit best?
options: Too much right rudder, and too little back pressure
Chasing the airspeed, and too much nose-up trim
Too little right rudder, and fixating on the nose
Too much forward pressure during the level-off
quiz.why: Yaw from inadequate right rudder and a wing-low climb from nose fixation are both on the list [[24:81|AFH 3-20]].

quiz.q: Your learner fixates on the attitude indicator in climbs. Which AFH tool targets that habit?
options: Rudder trim set for the climb speed before entry
Instrument covers that force outside references
A steeper climb so the nose is easier to see
Teaching climbing turns before straight climbs
quiz.why: Instructors may use instrument covers to break a habit of fixating on the instruments [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].

final_quiz.q: Halfway up a VY climb in a fixed-pitch trainer, RPM has fallen about 100 below the climb setting with the throttle unchanged. What do you teach?
options: The propeller is overspeeding; pull the throttle back to protect it
The mixture is too rich; lean it until RPM returns to the setting
The tachometer lags in climbs; ignore it until the level-off
Air is thinner aloft; advance the throttle to hold climb power
final_quiz.why: A normally aspirated engine loses power with altitude, shown by falling RPM with a fixed-pitch propeller, so the pilot keeps advancing the throttle to hold climb power [[24:80|AFH 3-19]].

final_quiz.q: The learner holds the climb picture but the airspeed settles 10 knots slow with climb power set, and reaches for the throttle. Your coaching?
options: Lower the nose slightly; with climb power fixed, pitch controls the airspeed
Add full power; in a climb airspeed is controlled with the throttle alone
Retrim nose-down first and let the airspeed find its own value
Raise the nose slightly so the wing makes more lift and more speed
final_quiz.why: Power stays at climb power and airspeed is controlled with elevator [[24:80|AFH 3-19]].

final_quiz.q: Climbing at 900 fpm to 7,500 feet, where does the level-off start, and what does the power do first?
options: About 7,410 feet; reduce to cruise power as the nose comes down
About 7,490 feet; climb power stays in until cruise airspeed
About 7,410 feet; climb power stays in until cruise airspeed
About 7,300 feet; reduce power first, then lower the nose
final_quiz.why: 10 percent of 900 fpm = 90 feet, so 7,500 - 90 = 7,410 feet. Climb power is kept until cruise airspeed, then cruise power and retrim [[24:81|AFH 3-20]].

final_quiz.q: In a left climbing turn your learner holds the same right rudder that worked well in the right climbing turn. What do you expect to see?
options: A skid, because rolling left needs much more right rudder than rolling right
A slip, because rolling left needs less right rudder than rolling right
No change, because rudder needs match in both directions in a climb
An overbank, because the left wing becomes the outside wing in the turn
final_quiz.why: Rolling left, P-factor cancels some adverse yaw, so less right rudder is needed [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]. Too much right rudder in a left turn yaws the nose to the outside: a slip, ball to the inside [[24:74|AFH 3-13]].

final_quiz.q: In a 30° climbing turn the learner keeps the straight-climb pitch and power. What happens, per the AFH?
options: The climb rate rises because the bank adds to the vertical lift component
Nothing changes as long as the ball stays centered in the turn
The airspeed rises because induced drag falls once the wings are banked
The climb angle gets shallower because some lift is turning the airplane
final_quiz.why: With constant power the same pitch and airspeed cannot be held in a bank; the airplane climbs at a slightly shallower angle because some lift turns it [[24:81|AFH 3-20]].

final_quiz.q: At high weight on a hot day, your learner tries a 35° climbing turn at VY and gets almost no climb. Best explanation?
options: Weight and density altitude cut excess power, and the steeper bank cuts climb more
VY rises with altitude, so the learner is now flying too slowly to climb at all
The overbanking tendency at 35° is draining the climb rate away in the turn
P-factor at high power is strongest in turns and robs the climb rate away
final_quiz.why: Weight and altitude reduce excess power and climb performance [[1:264|PHAK 11-8]], and steep banks significantly reduce the climb rate [[24:81|AFH 3-20]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner makes every pitch correction while looking at the attitude indicator, and the nose overshoots. Per the AFH, what is the fix?
options: Use the VSI as the primary pitch reference throughout the climb
Trim for every correction so the airplane holds each new attitude
Set pitch on the natural horizon, then glance inside to confirm
Use larger pitch corrections so the attitude indicator can show them
final_quiz.why: Correcting while looking inside is the most common beginner error; the horizon gives indications many times larger than any instrument [[24:67|AFH 3-6]].

final_quiz.q: On a long VY climb out of a nontowered airport, which collision-avoidance habit should you build?
options: A level-off every 500 feet to look for traffic straight ahead
Gentle banks left and right at intervals to scan ahead of the nose
Climbing at VX to spend less time below 1,000 feet above the ground
Watching the ADS-B In display full time, since it shows all aircraft nearby
final_quiz.why: The AIM calls for gentle banks during climbs to permit continuous scanning [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15]]; not every aircraft appears on ADS-B In [[33:287|AIM 4-4-15]].

final_quiz.q: During a climbing turn you ask the learner to find a frequency on the chart. The nose creeps up and the stall warning chirps. What is this showing?
options: The leans, from a slow turn that went below the detection threshold
Gyroscopic precession pitching the nose up as the turn develops
The overbanking tendency pulling the nose up above the horizon
A secondary task in a climb raising the risk of an inadvertent stall
final_quiz.why: Tasks secondary to aircraft control raise the risk of an inadvertent stall [[25:180|AIH 9-10]]; climbs and climbing turns are where accidental power-on stalls occur [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].

final_quiz.q: At level-off your learner pushes the nose down hard and says it felt like tumbling backward. What do you explain?
options: The inversion illusion; make the level-off smooth and slower
The elevator illusion; it comes from flying into an updraft
The somatogravic illusion; it comes from a rapid deceleration
The leans; it follows a gradual turn that went unnoticed
final_quiz.why: An abrupt change from climb to level flight can cause the inversion illusion [[1:430|PHAK 17-8]]. The AFH has the nose lowered smoothly and slowly [[24:81|AFH 3-20]].

final_quiz.q: Playing your learner, the examiner climbs with the nose well above the normal climb picture and the airspeed sinking. Which AFH error, and what fix?
options: Chasing the airspeed; hold the nose fixed and add more power
A deliberate VX climb; that is correct technique whenever obstacles exist
Too aggressive elevator; return smoothly to the known climb attitude
Too little right rudder; add rudder until the nose comes back down
final_quiz.why: Applying elevator too aggressively gives an excessive climb angle [[24:81|AFH 3-20]]; enter with gentle back pressure to the climb attitude [[24:80|AFH 3-19]].

final_quiz.q: Your learner trims constantly while the airspeed is still changing during climb entry. What does the AFH say?
options: Trim the rudder first and the elevator second at every airspeed change
Set and hold the attitude first, then trim off the remaining pressure
Trim continuously until the VSI settles, then hold the attitude
Leave trim at the cruise setting and hold the back pressure
final_quiz.why: Establish the attitude, hold it with control pressure, then trim the pressure out; trimming rudder while airspeed varies only adds workload [[24:71|AFH 3-10]].

final_quiz.q: Per the PHAK, which explanation of why a climb needs more power would you give a learner?
options: Part of the weight acts rearward along the path, adding to drag
Propeller efficiency falls by half in any nose-up attitude
Air is thinner above the airplane than below it in a climb
Induced drag doubles at the climb attitude, so thrust must double
final_quiz.why: On an upward path a component of weight acts with drag, so more power is needed to hold the same airspeed [[1:121|PHAK 5-24]].

takeaways: Climb entry: nose up and climb power together, right rudder, then trim; with power fixed, pitch controls airspeed [[24:80|AFH 3-19]].
A sustained climb needs excess thrust; the wing's lift is about the same as in level flight [[1:121|PHAK 5-24]].
Cruise climb for cooling and visibility, VY for time, VX for obstacles; check the POH for the day [[24:78|AFH 3-17]].
Climbing turns: shallow, constant bank, a little more back pressure, more right rudder rolling right [[24:81|AFH 3-20]] [[24:216|AFH 10-7]].
Level off at 10 percent of the climb rate, smoothly, and keep climb power until cruise speed [[24:81|AFH 3-20]].
Gentle banks during climbs keep the sky ahead of the nose in the scan [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15]].
Teach straight climbs before climbing turns, both directions, and add distractions only once the climb is consistent [[25:177|AIH 9-7]] [[25:75|AIH 3-24]].
cfi_notes: The CFI ACS gives no tolerances for any Area VIII Task. Brief your own standard (for example, airspeed and level-off targets from your syllabus) so the learner knows what "done" means [[25:175|AIH 9-5]].

The sources describe the climb's forces differently. The AFH says a climb needs excess lift and more power for the added induced drag [[24:78|AFH 3-17]] [[24:80|AFH 3-19]]; the PHAK says lift in a steady climb is about the same as level flight, with weight adding to drag [[1:120|PHAK 5-23]] [[1:121|PHAK 5-24]]. Both agree the climb is sustained by excess thrust; teach that, and expect learners who read the AFH line to ask.

PHAK 5-31 says the corkscrew slipstream's rolling moment is to the right while torque reaction's moment is to the left, and that one may partly cancel the other [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]]. The AFH simply says torque and P-factor roll and yaw the airplane left in the climb [[24:80|AFH 3-19]]. Teach the AFH net effect and the PHAK point that the pilot corrects whatever is strongest at the time.

Both the AFH and the IFH give the 10 percent level-off lead [[24:81|AFH 3-20]] [[23:177|IFH 7-16]]. The IFH adds a second technique, leveling at climb airspeed by reducing power with the pitch change; know both and say which you are teaching.
The AFH climb page focuses on pitch and power; the clearing in climbs comes from the AIM (gentle banks, verbal "clear" calls) [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15]]. Build it into the maneuver, not just before it.

Rudder needs differ left and right in climbing turns [[24:216|AFH 10-7]], and from the left seat the nose seems higher in left turns and lower in right turns [[24:76|AFH 3-15]]. Expect a learner to be good one way and not the other, and practice both.
The AIH distraction list includes "climb 200 feet and maintain altitude, then descend 200 feet" [[25:180|AIH 9-10]]: a ready-made way to fold this Task into later lessons.

The AIM says to make gentle banks during climbs and descents [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15]], while AC 90-48E suggests adjusting pitch to see over the nose in a climb and gentle banks in cruise or descent [[16:13|AC 90-48E 12.1]]. They do not conflict: teach both in the climb.
The AFH uses "beginner pilot" and "student"; the AIH uses "learner". Same person.
gaps: Climb power settings, pitch attitudes, cruise climb speed, VX and VY, cowl flap use and engine temperature limits are airplane-specific: use the POH/AFM.
The CFI ACS gives no numeric tolerances for this Task; the standard is set by the instructor or the training syllabus.
The AFH says to keep climbing turns shallow but gives no bank number for training, apart from the 15° to 20° used for power-on stall practice [[24:123|AFH 5-18]].
The AIM asks for gentle banks during climbs "at a frequency which permits continuous visual scanning" but gives no interval or bank angle [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15]].
No source says how much to lower the nose, or how often, to look over it during a climb; AC 90-48E only says to adjust the pitch attitude [[16:13|AC 90-48E 12.1]].

activities.title: Which climb fits?
activities.intro: Tap a situation, then tap the climb it calls for.

items.t: Long climb to cruise altitude, engine temperatures rising
Better view over the nose for traffic en route
More control authority wanted during the climb
Leaving a runway with no obstructions, until it is safe to transition
Reach an assigned altitude in the least time
A strand of trees beyond the departure end
Most altitude for the ground distance covered

activities.title: Straight climb from cruise
activities.intro: Use the arrows to put the climb entry in order, then tap Check.
steps: Raise the nose to the climb attitude while adding climb power
Right rudder for the left-turning tendencies
Hold the attitude as the airspeed settles
Cross-check instruments; keep advancing the throttle as power falls with altitude

activities.title: True or false: left-turning tendencies
activities.intro: Decide if each statement is true or false.

cards.s: At high angle of attack, P-factor moves the center of thrust to the right and yaws the nose left.
Built-in torque compensation is usually set for climb speed, since climbs are the critical phase.
cards.why: False. It is usually set for cruise speed, where the airplane spends most of its time [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]].

cards.s: With a clockwise propeller, torque reaction tends to roll the airplane to the left.
The spiraling slipstream gets stronger as forward speed increases.
cards.why: False. As speed increases the spiral elongates and becomes less effective [[1:128|PHAK 5-31]].

cards.s: Gyroscopic precession acts 90° ahead of the applied force, in the direction of rotation.
Trimming the rudder while airspeed is still changing reduces workload in a climb entry.
cards.why: False. It produces unnecessary workload and distraction [[24:71|AFH 3-10]].

activities.title: Read the climbing-turn entry
activities.intro: Tap a sign, then tap what it means.

pairs.l: Nose moves before the bank starts
Bank starts before the nose moves
Nose rises or drops as the bank starts
pairs.r: Too much or too little back pressure

pairs.l: Pressed toward the outside of the turn
Pressed toward the inside of the turn
Bank keeps steepening with ailerons neutral past about 45°

activities.title: Climb and level-off numbers
activities.intro: Work each one out, then type your answer.

items.q: Climbing at 700 fpm to level at 5,500 feet. Using the 10 percent rule, at what altitude does the level-off begin?
The VSI shows 450 fpm. How many feet before the target altitude should the level-off start?
A 10° climb needs thrust equal to drag plus 17 percent of weight. For a 2,300-pound airplane, how many pounds of thrust beyond drag is that?
In the PHAK example, the maximum rate of climb profile gains 1,500 feet in 30 seconds. What is that in feet per minute?
Same example: max angle profile gains 1,000 feet over 3,000 feet of ground; max rate profile gains 1,500 feet over 6,000 feet. How many feet does the max rate profile gain per 1,000 feet of ground?
items.why: 1,500 / 6,000 x 1,000 = 250 feet, against 1,000 / 3,000 x 1,000 = 333 feet for max angle, which is why VX clears obstacles [[1:263|PHAK 11-7]] [[1:264|PHAK 11-8]].

activities.title: Read the climb panel
activities.intro: Drag each description to the instrument that shows it in Figure 3-21 (left panel).

pins.label: Airspeed, set by pitch in the climb
Heading held in a straight climb

activities.title: First climbing-turn lesson
activities.intro: You are the instructor. Your learner flies good straight-and-level and level turns. Today is climbs and climbing turns. The lesson unfolds one decision at a time.

steps.s: On the ground the learner asks what "good" looks like, since the ACS has no tolerance for this Task. What do you brief?
options: Nothing yet; standards come after the first try so the learner feels no pressure
Only the VY number from the POH, since everything else follows from it
Your completion standards, the climb power and nose picture, the level-off lead and the clearing plan
The private pilot steep turn tolerances, since they are close enough to use
steps.why: The explanation phase covers objectives and completion standards, steps, end result and safety [[25:175|AIH 9-5]]; the pilot should know the power, attitude and instrument picture for each climb [[24:78|AFH 3-17]] and the level-off lead [[24:81|AFH 3-20]].

steps.s: In the practice area, before the first climb, what comes first?
options: A straight climb right away to save time, since the area looks empty
Clearing turns, with the learner calling "clear" out loud
Setting up the ADS-B display and relying on it for traffic
A climbing turn first, so the turn itself clears the area
steps.why: Clear before every training maneuver [[24:33|AFH 1-12]] and have learners verbalize "clear" [[33:286|AIM 4-4-15]].

steps.s: In your demo, power comes in and the nose rises past the picture you described. What now?
options: Say so right away, explain the slipstream pitch-up, then correct it
Say nothing so the learner keeps confidence in the demonstration
Start the demonstration over later without any comment on it
Let the learner fix it to see whether they notice the problem
steps.why: A deviation from the explanation should be acknowledged and explained at once [[25:177|AIH 9-7]]; added slipstream over the tail can raise the nose more than desired [[24:80|AFH 3-19]].

steps.s: Right climbing turns are now coordinated, but in left ones the ball sits toward the low wing with lots of right rudder held. Your fix?
options: More right rudder rolling left; P-factor adds to the adverse yaw
Aileron only, and ignore the ball until the climb is established
Skip left climbing turns until the next lesson to keep it simple
Less right rudder rolling left; P-factor cancels some adverse yaw
steps.why: Rolling left needs less right rudder than rolling right [[24:216|AFH 10-7]]; ball to the inside is a slip [[24:74|AFH 3-13]]. Practice both directions [[24:78|AFH 3-17]].

steps.s: The learner is consistent in both directions. What is the next step?
options: Add distractions, such as reading the OAT during a climbing turn
End the climbs block for good, since the skill is now learned
Move to VX climbing turns at 45° of bank for a challenge
Fly every remaining climb under a view-limiting device
steps.why: Distractions train divided attention [[25:180|AIH 9-10]] and are best added once the learner is past the cognitive stage [[25:75|AIH 3-24]].
